extracted.intended_audience: general readers and fans of Saturday Night Live, TV/comedy history readers
extracted.subtask_description: A feature-style retrospective recounting instances when performers uttered the F-word on Saturday Night Live, describing context, censorship, reactions, and downstream effects. Focuses on notable episodes, musical performances, cast slips, and how networks handled each incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionality (intent vs slip)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the F-word was improvised/accidental or deliberate/planned for the performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article distinguishes slips (e.g., Charles Rocket's improvised 'who the fuck did it?' and Paul Shaffer's on-air slip in 'Medieval Band') from intentional inclusions (e.g., Samuel L. Jackson was supposed to say 'Man, fuck you!' to be bleeped). Intent affects how producers and audiences judge the incident and what corrective actions are taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer/source type
rubrics_metrics.description: Who uttered the F-word — cast member, guest host, musical guest, band member, or cameo actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different performer types produce different patterns of incidents: cast members (e.g., Norm MacDonald, Sam Rockwell) may flub lines during sketches; musical guests (e.g., Prince, Steven Tyler, REM) may sing uncensored lyrics; guest stars (e.g., Samuel L. Jackson) may be expected to use stronger language. The article lists many examples tied to performer role to show likelihood and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live vs delayed broadcast / time-zone handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the episode aired live coast-to-coast or used delayed feeds (Mountain/Pacific delays) which affect censoring ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sam Rockwell's F-bomb occurred on one of the first episodes airing live across the country; previously delayed West Coast feeds allowed a few seconds to catch and mute profanity. The presence or absence of delays determines whether censor staff can bleep/mute in real time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship outcome (bleep, mute, or unedited)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the profanity was handled in the broadcast or later releases: bleeped, muted, left intact, or edited out entirely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kristen Stewart's 'coolest fucking thing' is audibly bleeped on streaming; Samuel L. Jackson's lines were muted due to an audio mistake; System Of A Down agreed to have F-bombs bleeped but a 'Fuck yeah!' slipped past the censor. Some sketches/performances are later edited out of streaming versions (Jenny Slate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and public reaction (calls, support/opposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The level and tenor of viewer response after an incident — number of complaints, supportive calls, or public controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes NBC received only five calls after Norm MacDonald's slip, three of which were supportive. Some incidents caused more uproar historically (Charles Rocket's aftermath), while others produced little measurable fallout (Metallica, James Hetfield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Career impact and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the utterance produced significant professional repercussions for the performer (firing, reputation damage, or no real effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charles Rocket faced meetings with NBC executives and later was fired (among other cast changes), but the piece argues saying 'fuck' was 'not quite the career-ender' — Rocket continued to work. Jenny Slate's later contract non-renewal is explicitly not attributed to her F-bomb. Assess incidents on a case-by-case basis; context and other factors matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control room and production responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of producers, network executives, and audio technicians in preventing or remedying on-air profanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes control-room decisions (e.g., instructing Tilton to improvise), producer permissions (Lorne Michaels allowing System Of A Down to sing unaltered but bleeped), and failures (an audio technician failed to bleep Samuel L. Jackson). Producer and technical staff actions determine whether profanity reaches audiences and how it is subsequently treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music-licensing and editorial cuts from archives/streaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-profanity editorial reasons (like music rights) that lead to segments being cut from streaming versions, which can affect whether F-bomb incidents remain available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sketch containing Charles Rocket's shooting was excised from Peacock likely due to Eric Clapton's 'After Midnight' music rights, yet the Good Night sequence with the F-bomb remains. The article also notes music performances from seasons 6–40 are cut from streaming because of licensing costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context within sketch or performance
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative or comedic framing when the profanity occurs — e.g., as part of a recurring running gag, a character moment, a song lyric, or a closing 'Good night' line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context shapes audience reaction and producer decisions: Rocket's F-bomb came during a running 'Who Shot Charles Rocket?' gag; Paul Shaffer's slip occurred inside a 'Medieval Band' sketch; Jenny Slate's slip happened in a 'Biker Chick Chat' bit where cursing is part of the conceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyric-based slips vs spoken-line slips
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the profanity appears in song lyrics (musical performance) or in spoken/sketch dialogue, which affects likelihood and reason for slips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musical guests often perform rehearsed songs and may 'slip' a swear that is part of lyrics (Prince's 'Partyup', Steven Tyler, REM, Beastie Boys). The article explains this is 'inevitable' given how often musicians perform songs and the pressure of live TV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterns and clustering over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal patterns (years or seasons with multiple incidents) and anomalous clusters of profanity occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1994 is highlighted as a year with three F-bombs within seven months (Janet Jackson, REM, Beastie Boys). Such clusters are noteworthy in historical retrospectives and may indicate shifting norms or random clustering rather than constant frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and form of historical record (edited vs unedited archives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the incident can be viewed today, and if so, whether it appears as originally aired, muted, bleeped, or edited out in streaming/archives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece emphasizes that some moments are intact on available streams (Charles Rocket's Good Night), others are muted/bleeped (Samuel L. Jackson, Kristen Stewart), and some sketches are omitted entirely from streaming platforms (Jenny Slate's sketch). Archivability affects how incidents are remembered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network policy and producer discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal and informal policies that govern how profanity is handled, including negotiated allowances and executive responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lorne Michaels negotiated with System Of A Down to allow an unaltered performance if bleeped for air. NBC executives called Rocket to apologize; Doumanian was later fired (though not solely for profanity). The article shows that policy application varies with producer judgment, guest agreements, and executive priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity and cultural infamy potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a profanity incident attains lasting notoriety and enters show lore or celebrity narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charles Rocket's utterance is described as earning him 'a rather infamous place in the show's history.' The article treats some incidents as moment-defining anecdotes that contribute to SNL's legend and collective memory.
